lead: Physical links are classified as guided (wired) or unguided (wireless). Guided media keep the signal inside a physical conductor, giving predictable loss and high bandwidth. Unguided media let the signal travel through air or space, offering mobility but higher attenuation. Choosing the right type decides whether a LAN in a Chennai apartment, a campus backbone, or a satellite link for remote villages works reliably.
prereq: You need: Analog and digital signals, Transmission impairments and Data rate limits.

blocks.text: Guided media use a physical path to confine the electromagnetic wave. The three most common types are twisted‑pair copper, coaxial cable and optical fibre.

items: Twisted‑pair: two insulated copper wires twisted together. Category 5e (Cat5e) supports up to 100 m at 1 Gbps. Attenuation ≈ 22 dB/100 m at 100 MHz.
Coaxial: inner conductor, dielectric, metallic shield, outer jacket. Used for cable TV and older Ethernet (10BASE‑2). Bandwidth up to 10 GHz, attenuation ≈ 6 dB/100 m at 1 GHz.

Optical fibre: glass core guiding light by total internal reflection. Single‑mode (core ≈ 9 µm) carries long distances with low loss (≈ 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm). Multimode (core ≈ 50 µm) is cheaper for short runs (≤ 2 km) but higher modal dispersion.

blocks.where: A is attenuation in dB; P₀ is transmitted power; P₁ is received power.

blocks.text: Attenuation expressed in dB adds linearly with distance for copper cables, but fibre loss is so small that repeaters are needed only after many kilometres.
Unguided media transmit through free space. The main categories are radio, microwave and satellite links; infrared is used for short‑range line‑of‑sight links such as TV remotes.

items: Radio: frequencies from a few kHz up to 3 GHz. Used for Wi‑Fi (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz) and cellular (LTE, 5G). Bandwidth can reach several hundred MHz, but path loss follows the free‑space model.
Microwave: 3 GHz–30 GHz, highly directional parabolic antennas. Ideal for point‑to‑point links between towers, e.g., a 10 km backhaul with 1 Gbps capacity.
Satellite: 4 GHz–40 GHz bands (C, Ku, Ka). Provides coverage over thousands of kilometres. Latency is high (≈ 500 ms) because of the round‑trip to geostationary orbit.
Infrared: 300 THz–400 THz, line‑of‑sight only, typical range < 5 m. Used in remote controls and some indoor data links.

blocks.where: FSPL is free‑space path loss in dB; d is distance in km; f is frequency in MHz.

blocks.text: FSPL shows why higher frequencies need more power or higher‑gain antennas for the same range.

Guided media are preferred when a stable, high‑capacity link is required and a physical path can be laid, such as campus LANs or fiber‑to‑the‑home. Unguided media are chosen for mobility, rapid deployment, or when wiring is impractical, for example, connecting a mobile handset to a 4G base station.

items: Check the maximum distance without repeaters.
Consider installation cost and environmental constraints.

Select guided media when a physical path can be laid and the required distance is within the practical reach of the chosen guided medium (e.g., up to 100 m for copper, up to many kilometres for fibre). Otherwise consider unguided media.

examples.question: A campus network uses a 100 m Cat5e cable for a workstation and a 10 km single‑mode fibre link to the main server. The Cat5e link supports 1 Gbps, while the fibre link supports 10 Gbps. What is the ratio of the maximum data rates of the fibre link to the copper link?
steps: Maximum data rate of Cat5e = 1 Gbps.
Maximum data rate of single‑mode fibre = 10 Gbps.
Ratio = fibre rate ÷ copper rate = 10 Gbps ÷ 1 Gbps = 10.
examples.answer: The fibre link can carry ten times the data rate of the Cat5e copper link.
examples.check:
rate_copper = 1e9
rate_fibre = 10e9
ratio = rate_fibre / rate_copper
print(ratio)

traps: Assuming attenuation of all guided media is the same per kilometre; copper loss is much higher than fibre loss.
Confusing bandwidth (Hz) with data rate (bits/s); they are related but not identical.
Microwave links typically use frequencies up to 30 GHz. Satellite communications use portions of this range (C‑band 4‑8 GHz, Ku‑band 12‑18 GHz) and also higher bands such as Ka (≈ 26‑40 GHz).
Using the free‑space path loss formula for a guided copper link; FSPL applies only to unguided propagation.
Mistaking multimode fibre for single‑mode and assuming the same maximum distance without repeaters.

quiz.q: Name the three common guided transmission media.
quiz.a: Twisted‑pair, coaxial cable, and optical fibre.

quiz.q: Why does single‑mode fibre allow longer distances than multimode fibre?
quiz.a: Single‑mode fibre has a very small core that supports only one propagation mode, eliminating modal dispersion and therefore preserving signal integrity over many kilometres.

quiz.q: If a Wi‑Fi link at 5 GHz suffers 80 dB path loss, what is the required antenna gain (in dBi) assuming transmitter power is 20 dBm and receiver sensitivity is –90 dBm?
quiz.a: Link budget: required total gain = 80 dB + (‑90 dBm) – 20 dBm = ‑30 dBi. This means no extra antenna gain is needed; any positive‑gain antenna will satisfy the link budget. If a margin of 30 dB is desired, total antenna gain of at least 30 dBi is required.

quiz.q: A company must connect two offices 8 km apart. They can choose either a 10 Gbps single‑mode fibre link (cost ₹2 lakh per km) or a microwave point‑to‑point link (cost ₹5 lakh for equipment plus ₹0.5 lakh per km for mounting). Which option is cheaper and by how much?
quiz.a: Fibre cost = 8 km × 2 lakh = ₹16 lakh. Microwave cost = ₹5 lakh + (8 km × 0.5 lakh) = ₹5 lakh + ₹4 lakh = ₹9 lakh. Microwave is cheaper by ₹7 lakh.

quiz.q: Calculate the free‑space path loss for a 2 km link operating at 2.4 GHz. Give the result in dB.
quiz.a: Convert frequency: f = 2400 MHz. Use FSPL(d) = 20 log₁₀(d) + 20 log₁₀(f) + 32.44 = 20 log₁₀(2) + 20 log₁₀(2400) + 32.44 ≈ 6.02 + 67.60 + 32.44 = 106.06 dB.

quiz.q: A designer must choose between twisted‑pair and fibre for a 150 m link carrying 1 Gbps video. The budget allows up to ₹5 lakh. Which medium should be selected and why?
quiz.a: Twisted‑pair (Cat5e) supports 1 Gbps up to 100 m only; 150 m exceeds its limit, requiring a repeater that adds cost and latency. Fibre (multimode) supports 1 Gbps over many kilometres and the cost of 150 m multimode fibre plus connectors is well under ₹5 lakh. Therefore fibre is the appropriate choice.

quiz.q: List two frequency ranges used for satellite communications.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, guided media are evolving with 400 Gbps Ethernet over multimode fibre for data‑center interconnects. Research on hollow‑core photonic bandgap fibre aims to reduce latency below that of copper. Wireless 5G uses millimetre‑wave (mmWave) bands, blurring the line between traditional microwave and optical backhaul. Future curricula add topics on Li‑Fi (light‑based Wi‑Fi) and satellite constellations like Starlink. Searching "optical OFDM" and "massive MIMO" will reveal the next generation of high‑speed transmission technologies.
